In clean/onion architecture, dependencies always point inward, so inner layers (domain) have no knowledge of outer layers.
Domain entities should be framework-agnostic and persist-layer-agnostic, depending only on PHP itself (and possibly the standard library).
Controllers and templates belong to the delivery/presentation layer; the business logic resides in use cases (application/domain layer) which they merely invoke.
The center of the onion architecture contains the domain model (entities), with services, application services, and outer layers built around it.
Static analysis tools like deptrac detect forbidden layer dependencies automatically and fail the build.
A use case should accept only primitive/domain objects, not framework or infrastructure artifacts like HTTP requests or an EntityManager, to remain decoupled from delivery and persistence mechanisms.
A Repository provides a collection-like interface over aggregates/entities while abstracting the storage mechanism.
Database details belong to the outer infrastructure layer, so replacing the database does not affect the inner domain and use-case layers.
An aggregate is a domain model concept: a cluster of entities and value objects treated as a consistency boundary, not merely a database table.
Value Objects are defined by immutability and equality based on field values rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single entry point through which all changes to an aggregate must pass.
Repositories provide persistence access per aggregate root; entities inside an aggregate are reached through the root.
Ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary used by developers and domain experts in Domain-Driven Design to build the model.
It is the domain of discourse (universe) that bounds the set of objects a model and its language consistently refer to.
DDD recommends a rich domain model where behavior lives inside entities, not in anemic objects handled entirely by services.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a model applies, so the same concept (e.g., 'Customer') can be represented by different classes in different contexts.
